name: Cimmerians
info: The Cimmerians were an Eastern Iranic equestrian nomadic people of the Caspian and Ciscaucasian steppes who crossed the Caucasus in the 8th century BC and shook Urartu, Phrygia, Lydia and the Neo-Assyrian Empire.

facts.homeland: the Caspian and Ciscaucasian steppes north of the Caspian Sea, between the Araxes (Volga) and the Cimmerian Bosporus (Kerch Strait), in present-day Southern Russia; later māt Gamir around Gori in Georgia, then Cappadocia and Central Anatolia, with a capital at Ḫarzallē, and an eastern group near Mannai and Media
facts.period: part of the Chernogorovka-Novocherkassk complex (9th to mid-7th centuries BC); in Transcaucasia from c. 750 BC; first recorded in 714 BC; division into western and eastern groups under Esarhaddon (681–669 BC); the height of power under Dugdammî, called 'King of the Universe' by 657 BC; final defeat around c. 635 BC
facts.known: mounted archery with Scythian-type socketed arrowheads and sigmoid bows; the defeat of Rusa I of Urartu; the sack of Gordion and the fall of Phrygia; the sack of Sardis in 644 BC and the death of Gyges; the destruction of the Artemision of Ephesus; Animal Style art; bringing trousers to Central Europe
facts.sources: no written records of their own; Neo-Assyrian records of the 8th to 7th centuries BC (intelligence reports, oracle texts, royal inscriptions); Graeco-Roman authors from Homer and Herodotus to Strabo; the Hebrew Bible as Gōmer; kurgans, weapons and horse gear from the steppe, Caucasia and Anatolia; genetic studies of 2018 and 2019

t: The Cimmerians were culturally and archaeologically indistinguishable from the Scythians, yet every source of their own time treated them as a separate people.
After crossing the Caucasus they defeated Urartu, destroyed the empire of Phrygia, sacked Sardis and for a time ended Neo-Assyrian control in Anatolia, helping the Medes and Lydians rise.
Around c. 635 BC the Scythians under Madyes and the Lydians under Alyattes defeated them, and they disappeared from history, assimilated by the peoples of Anatolia.
dyk: By 657 BC an Assyrian astrologer was calling the Cimmerian king Dugdammî šar-kiššati, 'King of the Universe', a title normally held only by the king of Assyria and given to no other foreign ruler in the empire's history.
ev: The Cimmerians help Colchis and nearby regions defeat attacks by Urartu
The Cimmerians heavily defeat Rusa I of Urartu, in the first recorded mention of them
Esarhaddon kills the Cimmerian king Teušpâ in a campaign in Cilicia
Under Dugdammî the western Cimmerians destroy the empire of Phrygia and sack Gordion
Gyges of Lydia defeats the Cimmerians and sends captured city-lords to Ashurbanipal
The Cimmerians and Treres capture Sardis except its citadel, and Gyges is killed
Dugdammî falls gravely ill on campaign and takes his own life in Cilicia
Scythians under Madyes and Lydians under Alyattes defeat the Cimmerians and Treres

sections.origins:
The Cimmerians belonged to the first wave of nomads who moved west from the region of eastern Kazakhstan or the Altai-Sayan between the 10th and the 9th to 8th centuries BC. True nomadic pastoralism had emerged at the start of the first millennium BC, when climatic change turned sedentary Bronze Age farmers into herders. In the Pontic-Caspian steppe these migrants formed the tribal confederations of the Chernogorovka-Novocherkassk complex, which drew on the native Bilozerka culture, on the Altai, Aržan and Karasuk cultures of Central Asia and Siberia, and on the Kuban culture of Ciscaucasia.

The Cimmerians lived in the Caspian and Ciscaucasian steppes, from the Araxes, that is the Volga, which divided them from the Scythians, west to the Bosporus, the Kerch Strait. The earlier claim that they lived in the Pontic Steppe lacks evidence; that region was held by the Agathyrsi. The origin of their name is uncertain: János Harmatta proposed Old Iranic *Gayamira, 'union of clans', while Askold Ivantchik derives it from *Gimĕr- or *Gimĭr-, reaching Greek through Lydian. Assyrian texts call them Gimirrāya.

They were an Iranic people who shared a language, origin and culture with the Scythians, though they may have been a mixed confederation under an Iranic aristocracy. A Thracian origin is considered untenable, arising from a confusion with their allies the Treres. Genetic studies of 2018 and 2019 examined remains of six Cimmerians, three of them buried between around 1000 and 800 BC.
sections.society:
The Cimmerians lived an equestrian nomadic pastoralist life like that of the Scythians. West Asian sources mention their arrows, bows and horse equipment, and they used the same horse harness and weapons as the Scythians and fought on horseback. The "mare-milkers" and "milk consumers" of Homer's Odyssey might have referred to them. Their mounted warfare was so effective that West Asian states adopted Scythian-type socketed arrowheads and sigmoid bows in the 7th and 6th centuries BC, and Assyrian sources speak of "Cimmerian bows" and "Cimmerian leather straps".

Like the Scythians, they were organised as a tribal nomadic state with its own boundaries. A supreme king ruled, his power passing within a single dynasty; three kings are known by name, Teušpâ, Dugdammî and Sandakšatru. The king could convene military assemblies of the troops, and warlords could rebel against him. The confederation may have been split into larger divisions as politics changed, much as the Xiongnu and the Oguz Turks were divided into wings.

In Anatolia the western group became sedentary. By c. 670 BC they ruled native settlements and had founded their own, some fortified, with Ḫarzallē as Dugdammî's capital. Each settlement had a ruler whom the Assyrians called a bēl ālāni, a 'city-lord', and these were both Cimmerians and members of other peoples of the kingdom. The Anatolian Cimmerians also took up chariot warfare and unmounted infantry. A later tradition held that they lived for a long time on the wheat stored in the underground granaries of the Phrygian village of Syassos.
sections.beliefs:
Very little is known of Cimmerian religion. They left no written records, and the Assyrian and Greek texts that mention them are concerned with war and diplomacy. The burial customs of the steppe complex to which they belonged show a strong impact of the native Bilozerka culture, and remains typical of Iron Age steppe nomads in Caucasia and Transcaucasia, including kurgans with weapons, horse harness and horses, might have belonged to them. Deer stone-like carved stelae are among the Inner Asian elements of the Chernogorovka-Novocherkassk complex.

The western Cimmerians who settled in West Asia appear to have adopted the worship of the Anatolian deity Šanta from the people of Ḫilakku and Tabal. The name of the god might appear as an element in the name of the king Sandakšatru. While they served as mercenaries of Urartu under Argišti II, some Cimmerians may have made the human funerary statues in the region of Muṣaṣir that resemble those of steppe nomads.

To their enemies the Cimmerians were outsiders who did not fear the Mesopotamian gods; Esarhaddon's adviser Bēl-ušēzib warned the king to spy on them. Assyrian kings sought through divination to learn whether the Cimmerians would invade again. In 652 BC an oracle told Ashurbanipal that the goddess Ishtar had promised their defeat, and after the death of Sandakšatru Ashurbanipal thanked the god Marduk for the fate that had struck him.
sections.arts:
The Cimmerians used the same Animal Style art as the Scythians. This art, together with dagger and arrowhead types and bits with stirrup-shaped terminals, came into the Chernogorovka-Novocherkassk complex from the Altai, Aržan and Karasuk cultures of Central Asia and Siberia, while mace heads and bimetallic daggers followed models of the Kuban culture of Ciscaucasia. Pottery styles show the influence of the native Bilozerka culture.

The Cimmerians were part of the Scytho-Siberian horizon, and their material culture was so close to that of the early Scythians that the Chernogorovka-Novocherkassk and Proto-Scythian cultures cannot be told apart. By the time they entered West Asia, both had developed into the Early Scythian culture. "Scythian" arrowheads have been found among the weapons of besieging armies at ruined cities in parts of Anatolia where Cimmerians, but not Scythians, are attested.

Their presence in Anatolia has still largely not been identified in the archaeology of the Iron Age. A burial at İmirler in the Amasya Province of Turkey holds Early Scythian weapons and horse harness, and another, about 100 km to the east of it, contained 250 Scythian-type arrowheads. Scythian-type animal style ornaments found at Büklükale might mark a Cimmerian settlement, though the identification is uncertain. The complex also left a lasting mark on the Hallstatt culture of Central Europe, which adopted trousers from the steppe nomads.
sections.exchange:
The Cimmerians entered West Asia across the Caucasus through the Alagir, Darial and Klukhor passes and first settled in central Transcaucasia, near modern Gori, which Mesopotamian sources called māt Gamir, 'the Land of the Cimmerians'. The rivalries of Assyria, Urartu, Phrygia and smaller states offered rich opportunities, and the Cimmerians served whoever paid them best. In 714 BC they routed Rusa I of Urartu, killing the governor of Uišini and capturing its commander in chief, which left Urartu open to Sargon II's campaign that year. Under Esarhaddon they split into a western group under Teušpâ in Anatolia and an eastern group, the Indaraeans, near Mannai.

The eastern Cimmerians allied with the Mannaean king Aḫšēri, deceived Esarhaddon after promising him neutrality, and sided with the Median leader Kaštaritu when he founded the first independent kingdom of the Medes. In the west, Dugdammî destroyed Phrygia around c. 675 BC, after which its king Midas killed himself, and by the early 660s BC the Cimmerians were masters of Anatolia. They destroyed the Greek colony of Sinope and killed its founder Habrōn, the first encounter between the Greeks and steppe nomads. Lydia under Gyges fought them off around c. 665–660 BC, but in 644 BC the Cimmerians and the Thracian Treres took Sardis, killed Gyges and went on to destroy Magnesia on the Meander and the Artemision of Ephesus.

Their power faded after Dugdammî's death in 640 BC. Around c. 635 BC the Scythians under Madyes and the Lydians under Alyattes defeated them for good.
sections.legacy:
After their final defeat the Cimmerians disappeared from history and were soon assimilated by the peoples and states of Anatolia, such as Lydia, Media and Pteria. Their inroads, with those of the Scythians, had upset the balance between Assyria, Urartu and Phrygia, brought several of these states down and opened the way for the empires of the Medes and the Lydians. They also made trade routes such as the Great Khorasan Road dangerous and spread steppe military technology across West Asia; the Lydians themselves took up mounted cavalry.

Their memory outlived them. Late Babylonian scribes of the Achaemenid Empire used the name Gimirri for all the steppe nomads, including the Saka, and the Hebrew Bible names them Gōmer, closely linked to ʾAškənāz, the Scythians. The Ionian Greeks long feared them: an inscription of 283 BC records Samos and Priene still disputing the territory of Batinētis abandoned during the invasion. In medieval Armenian tradition Cappadocia was called Gamirkʻ.

Homer's Odyssey placed the Cimmerians in a sunless land at the entrance of Hades, a poetic image that later writers moved to Italy, the far north or Hyperborea, and Posidonius equated them with the Cimbri. Herodotus's story of a royal tribe that fought itself to death is now read as a folk tale, and research in the late 20th century concluded that the "Cimmerian" place names of the Pontic Steppe were invented in the 6th century BC. The racialist and antisemitic British Israelist movement built a pseudohistory on them, and in fiction Robert E. Howard made Conan the Barbarian a Cimmerian.

summary: The Cimmerians were Iranic horse nomads of the Caspian steppe, close kin of the Scythians, who crossed the Caucasus in the 8th century BC. As raiders, mercenaries and conquerors they defeated Urartu, destroyed Phrygia and sacked Sardis, until the Scythians and Lydians defeated them around 635 BC; they then vanished into the peoples of Anatolia, leaving a long afterlife in legend.
